candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the request URL only (query parameter 'json'); they do not control the server-side code or victim credentials. The JSON contents (stapler-class, parameter names/values) are fully attacker-chosen, so the class to instantiate and its bound arguments are attacker-controlled. No Jenkins-side privilege beyond what the victim already has is needed to construct the request; the request is fired from a page the attacker controls and rides on the victim's existing session.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked for a permission/annotation that would neutralize the issue: there is no @RequirePOST, no Jenkins.RUN_SCRIPTS/Item.CONFIGURE check, and no POST-only Jelly/JS contract visible in this snapshot (the repo-side callers/views are absent from the pruned file set, and GENERATE_URL is consumed by pipeline-model-definition elsewhere). I verified that other mutating endpoints in the same plugin do carry @RequirePOST, so the omission is not a project-wide convention. I also confirmed the endpoint does not store the instantiated object (no persistence), so this is not a stored-configuration modification; impact is bounded by the side effects of installed Describable constructors/setters. Jenkins core does not apply a global CSRF token to read-style URLs, only @RequirePOST conventions, so a GET handler is reachable cross-site; however, modern browser SameSite cookie behavior may require a top-level navigation rather than an invisible subresource request.
candidates.impact: In the typical case this is a nuisance/CSRF issue: an attacker can make a victim's browser silently (or via navigation) instantiate arbitrary Describable/Step objects with attacker-chosen arguments, which can trigger plugin-defined constructor/setter side effects (e.g., validation logic, network/resource access, file or object creation, expensive work) inside the victim's authenticated session. Depending on which plugins with side-effecting descriptors/constructors are installed, the impact can rise from configuration confusion/denial of service to unintended operations; cross-origin response reading is not possible, so exfiltration is not demonstrated by source evidence alone. The fix pattern is the same one used elsewhere in this plugin: require POST (e.g., @RequirePOST) for the endpoint.
candidates.prerequisites: A victim user logged in to Jenkins with at least Overall/Read (and, for meaningful effect, permission to view the Pipeline Syntax page) must be lured into making a cross-site request to /pipeline-syntax/generateSnippet?json=...; the instance must have at least one Describable/Step descriptor whose constructor or @DataBoundSetter has security-relevant side effects, and browser cookie policy must still send the session cookie for the cross-site navigation (e.g., top-level navigation with SameSite=Lax). No attacker-side Jenkins account or API token is required beyond what is needed to host the lure.
candidates.root_cause: Snippetizer.doGenerateSnippet is exposed as a normal GET handler: it is annotated only with @Restricted(DoNotUse.class) (src/main/java/.../Snippetizer.java:486-487), with no @RequirePOST (and no other permission check). The method accepts attacker-controlled JSON via @QueryParameter String json, resolves an arbitrary class name to a Describable descriptor, and calls descriptor.newInstance(req, jsonO) to construct an object (lines 487-501), then serializes the constructed Step back to Groovy text (lines 502-527). Because the same plugin annotates its other side-effecting/instantiation endpoints with @RequirePOST (CpsFlowDefinition.DescriptorImpl.doCheckScript / doCheckScriptCompile, ReplayAction.doRun/doRebuild/doCheckScript/doCheckScriptCompile, PauseUnpauseAction.doToggle), the missing annotation on this endpoint is an inconsistent, source-verifiable gap rather than a deliberate read-only API.
candidates.title: Missing @RequirePOST on Snippetizer.doGenerateSnippet allows cross-site forced instantiation of arbitrary Describable/Step objects
candidates.trace: 1) Snippetizer is a RootAction (getUrlName() == 'pipeline-syntax', line 381-385) and GENERATE_URL is 'pipeline-syntax/generateSnippet' (line 483-484). 2) A cross-site GET to that URL reaches doGenerateSnippet (line 487) without any POST requirement or permission check. 3) It parses the JSON (line 489), loads the named class from the uber classloader and resolves the descriptor (lines 490-495). 4) It calls descriptor.newInstance(req, jsonO) (line 498), executing the Describable's data-bound construction/binding in the victim's session. 5) It then walks the resulting Step (lines 502-527) and returns generated Groovy text; the response body is not readable cross-origin, but the instantiation side effects have already occurred.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no request was executed and no Jenkins instance was contacted. I could not verify (a) whether upstream workflow-cps later added @RequirePOST to this method as a security fix (the snapshot is the pre-fix state per this review's assumption, but the fix commit was not inspected), (b) which specific installed plugin descriptors have exploitable constructor/setter side effects, or (c) the browser cookie policy (SameSite) on the target instance, which affects exploitability. If the endpoint is considered purely read-only by the Jenkins security model, severity drops to low. Sandbox-escape hypotheses (CpsWhitelist/GroovyClassLoaderWhitelist/DSL) were inspected but no concrete bypass was substantiated from source.
candidates.weakness_type: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on a GET-reachable object-instantiation endpoint (CWE-352)

coverage_summary: All 103 model-visible files were in scope (no files excluded by the safety filters). I read in full or in substantive part every main Java class related to execution/sandbox/security, including CpsFlowExecution, CpsGroovyShell(+Factory), CpsWhitelist, GroovyClassLoaderWhitelist, SandboxContinuable, CpsScript, CpsThread, CpsThreadGroup, CpsStepContext, DSL, ArgumentsActionImpl, EnvActionImpl, Snippetizer, ReplayAction and the replay package, CpsFlowDefinition(+Validator), CpsScmFlowDefinition, LoadStepExecution, ParallelStep(+Execution), RunningFlowActions, CpsThreadDumpAction, GlobalVariable/ParamsVariable/RunWrapperBinder, node classes, and the JS/HTML/Groovy resources. Only tests, views not present in the snapshot (e.g., .jelly), and third-party dependencies were outside the visible tree, so external libraries (script-security, groovy-cps, workflow-api/support, structs) were not inspected and their behavior is assumed from call sites.
limitations: No tests or .jelly/Stapler views are present in the snapshot, so server-side request handling and regression tests that may reveal the intended vulnerable path could not be inspected.

Third-party dependencies (script-security, groovy-cps, workflow-api/support, structs, Jenkins core) are not in the tree; sandbox internals such as GroovySandbox.createBaseCompilerConfiguration/createSecureClassLoader and Descriptor.newInstance behavior were reasoned about but not read.
Static review only: no code was executed, no Jenkins instance was queried, and no exploit payload was attempted, so the CSRF candidate is a source-based lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

No upstream history/diff was available, so I could not confirm which change upstream made after this snapshot; the choice of the strongest candidate is based on in-tree evidence and consistency with the plugin's own @RequirePOST conventions.

The snapshot's exact date/version is inferred only from dependency and workflow pins; this affects which real-world fix the snapshot precedes and therefore the confidence that the submitted candidate is the intended one.

rejected_leads.lead: ArgumentsActionImpl.sanitizeObjectAndRecordMutation sets isUnmodifiedBySanitization = true in the 'primitive arrays aren't a valid type' branch (src/main/java/.../arguments/ArgumentsActionImpl.java:239-241), where every sibling failure branch sets false.
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to be dead/unreachable code: primitive arrays already fail isStorableType() at line 224 (isStorableType returns false for arrays with primitive component type), so the branch is not exercised and isUnmodifiedArguments() is not observably wrong; no secret-masking bypass could be constructed from it.

rejected_leads.lead: Snippetizer.doGenerateSnippet loads an arbitrary class name from the plugin uber classloader and instantiates it without any explicit permission check.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the same root cause as the submitted candidate; the class load is constrained to Describable subclasses and object construction is confined to descriptors, so it is not a separate class-loading/RCE finding beyond the CSRF aspect already reported.

rejected_leads.lead: ReplayAction.doCheckScriptCompile delegates to CpsFlowDefinition.DescriptorImpl.doCheckScriptCompile with @AncestorInPath Item job and can NPE when job is null; CpsFlowDefinition.doCheckScriptCompile performs no null check on job.
rejected_leads.reason: A null job yields an HTTP 500/Stapler error rather than a permission bypass (the CONFIGURE check is not reachable with a null job, and no script is compiled when unauthorized), so no security impact was substantiated.

rejected_leads.lead: LoadStepExecution.start reads FilePath cwd.child(step.getPath()) with a path that may be absolute or contain '..', potentially reading files outside the workspace on the controller/agent.
rejected_leads.reason: Could not verify FilePath.child() absolute-path/.. semantics from this snapshot, the step requires a workspace context, and any user who can run the build there can generally read those files by other means; no clear privilege boundary crossing was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Candidates around the Groovy sandbox (CpsWhitelist.getProperty/invokeMethod grants, GroovyClassLoaderWhitelist classloader checks, SandboxContinuable/CpsGroovyShellFactory configuration).
rejected_leads.reason: Each grant was traced and is consistent with the documented trusted/untrusted classloader design (doc/classloader.md); no concrete sandbox escape could be demonstrated from source alone, so these were not promoted to a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: CpsThreadDumpAction exposes thread dumps to users who can view a build, and InterpolatedSecretsAction exposes secret variable names via its exported warnings.
rejected_leads.reason: These are informational surfaces tied to Item/Read on the build; no secret values are included by the source inspected, and program.xml already requires Jenkins.RUN_SCRIPTS, so no concrete disclosure was established.

summary: Reviewed the assigned 103-file workflow-cps (Pipeline: Groovy) snapshot. Coverage was a broad read of the main Java sources and resources: the CPS/sandbox machinery (CpsFlowExecution, CpsGroovyShell(+Factory), CpsWhitelist, GroovyClassLoaderWhitelist, SandboxContinuable, CpsThread/ThreadGroup/StepContext, DSL, CpsScript), ReplayAction and its factory/CLI, the Snippetizer web surface, ArgumentsActionImpl masking, EnvActionImpl, CpsScmFlowDefinition, steps (load/parallel), and view/JS resources. No source line was found that obviously grants sandbox escape, arbitrary code execution, or secret disclosure; the sandbox glue (CpsWhitelist, GroovyClassLoaderWhitelist, sandboxed re-parse of the main script and loaded scripts) is internally consistent with the documented design. The one concrete, evidence-backed weakness is that Snippetizer.doGenerateSnippet — which parses attacker-supplied JSON and instantiates arbitrary Describable/Step objects via Descriptor.newInstance — is reachable by GET because it lacks @RequirePOST, unlike every other state-changing/instantiation endpoint in this plugin. This is submitted as the single strongest candidate; it is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability, and its practical severity depends on installed plugins' constructor/setter side effects.
